title: Inversion of Object
statement:
Write `invertObject(obj)`. The argument `obj` is a JSON object or a JSON array whose values are all strings. Return a new object in which keys and values trade places: every distinct value of `obj` becomes a key of the result, and that key maps to the key of `obj` holding the value. When `obj` is an array, its keys are the indices written as strings (`"0"`, `"1"`, ...).

- If two or more keys of `obj` hold the same value, that value maps to an **array** of all of those keys, listed in the order of `Object.keys(obj)` (integer-like keys in ascending order first, then the other keys in their original order).
- A value held by exactly one key maps to that key as a plain string, not a one-element array.
- The result is always an object, even when `obj` is an array. The order of its keys does not matter.
constraints: obj is a JSON object or a JSON array
Every value in obj is a string
Neither a key nor a value of obj is "__proto__"
api: invertObject(obj: Record<string, string> | string[]): Record<string, string | string[]>
notes:
## Intuition

Inverting is a single pass: each entry `key -> value` of `obj` becomes `value -> key` in a new object. The only complication is a collision, when a second key holds a value already seen. The slot for that value then has to grow from a single string into an array, and every later key with the same value is appended to it. Because `Object.keys` works the same way for arrays (it lists the indices as strings), arrays need no special case. (The brute force instead collects, for each distinct value, every key holding it with a `filter`, which is simpler but quadratic.)

## Approach

1. Start with an empty object `inverted`.
2. Walk `Object.keys(obj)` in order and read each `value = obj[key]`.
3. If `inverted` has no own entry for `value`, store `key` there as a string.
4. Otherwise, if the entry is already an array, push `key` onto it.
5. Otherwise (it holds one string), replace it with the array `[old key, key]`.
6. Return `inverted`.

## Example 1, step by step

`obj = { a: "1", b: "2", c: "3", d: "4" }`.

- `a` holds `"1"`, which `inverted` does not have yet, so `inverted["1"] = "a"`.
- `b`, `c` and `d` do the same with `"2"`, `"3"` and `"4"`.
- No value repeats, so the answer is `{ "1": "a", "2": "b", "3": "c", "4": "d" }`.

In Example 2, `c` meets `"2"` again, so `inverted["2"]` changes from `"b"` to `["b", "c"]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) for n entries: each key is visited once and every update is O(1) (amortized for `push`).
- Space: O(n) for the inverted object.

## Pitfalls

- Testing `if (inverted[value])` instead of an own-property check: a value such as `""` would be stored and then look missing, and names like `"constructor"` look present through the prototype.
- Always wrapping keys in arrays: a value held once must map to a plain string.
- Overwriting on a collision (`inverted[value] = key`) silently loses the earlier keys.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `inverted` | the result: each value of `obj` mapped to its key or list of keys |
| `key` | the current key of `obj` (an index string for arrays) |
| `value` | the string `obj` holds at `key`, which becomes a key of `inverted` |

narration.1: invertObject builds a brand-new object instead of changing obj.
narration.2: inverted will map each value of obj back to the key, or keys, holding it.
narration.3: Object.keys lists the keys in order; for an array these are the indices as strings.
narration.4: value is the string stored under key, and it becomes a key of the result.
narration.5: An own-property check tells whether this value has been seen before, even for values like "" or "constructor".
narration.6: First time this value appears: it maps to this key as a plain string.
narration.7: The value has already collected two or more keys, so it holds an array.
narration.8: Append this key so the list keeps the order of obj.
narration.10: Second time the value appears: turn the single key into an array of both keys.
narration.13: Every entry has been flipped; return the inverted object.
